APE-001.q: An economy with very high trade openness (total trade well above GDP) like Vietnam is most sensitive to:
APE-001.e: Export orders, FDI and the exchange rate transmit external shocks quickly.
o: External demand swings and the global trade cycle
APE-001.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; statistics office data (Vietnam's trade/GDP around 160–190% in recent years).
Analysis: A very open economy: external demand and the global trade cycle transmit quickly via export orders, FDI flows, the exchange rate and import prices → most sensitive to external shocks (US/EU/China downturns, trade wars, the semiconductor cycle).
Distractors: B, C and D have small or local effects.
Note (FERGASITOR macro layer): track major partners' PMIs, export orders and US trade policy when assessing Vietnam's cycle.

APE-002.q: Exports USD 400 billion, imports 380 billion, GDP 470 billion. What is trade openness (trade/GDP, %, 2 decimals)?
APE-002.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (trade openness).
Working: Openness = (400 + 380) / 470 = 780 / 470 ≈ 165.96%.
Analysis: Trade is nearly 1.7× GDP – but much is imported inputs for exports (low domestic value added – APE-063), so high openness doesn't mean exports add equivalently to GDP (only net exports of 20 billion count).
Check: 470 × 1.6596 ≈ 780 ✓.

APE-003.q: The FDI sector accounts for most exports. Which implication matters when reading the balance of payments?
APE-003.e: Hence GNI is below GDP and domestic value added in exports is below gross export value.
o: A large trade surplus may be largely offset by a primary income deficit from FDI profit repatriation
Exports don't affect the exchange rate
The trade surplus always equals the current account surplus
APE-003.x:
Basis: IMF BPM6; SBV balance of payments data.
Analysis: The FDI sector accounts for about 70% of exports and most of the trade surplus; FDI profits repatriated to parents appear in primary income (large negative) → the goods surplus is substantially offset; the current account is much smaller (MCR-084). Consequences: GNI < GDP (MCR-007), and exports' domestic value added is below their gross value.
Distractors: B – exports supply FX; C – primary, secondary income and services also count; D is wrong.

APE-004.q: A sector's contribution to GDP growth is approximately its growth rate times its previous-period GDP share.
APE-004.e: True. Sector contributions sum to GDP growth.
APE-004.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (contributions to growth).
Analysis: True. Sector i's contribution (points) ≈ its previous-period GDP share × its growth rate. Contributions sum to GDP growth (APE-006). This shows which sectors really drive growth – fast growers with small shares contribute little.

APE-005.q: Industry and construction are 38% of GDP and grow 9%. What is their contribution to GDP growth (pp)?
APE-005.x:
Basis: SNA 2008.
Working: Contribution = 38% × 9% = 0.0342 = 3.42 points.
Analysis: Industry–construction, large and fast-growing, provides nearly half of 7.2% GDP growth (APE-006).

APE-006.q: Shares and growth: industry–construction 38% (9%); services 42% (7%); agriculture 12% (3%); product taxes less subsidies 8% (6%). What is GDP growth (%)?
APE-006.x:
Basis: SNA 2008 (production approach).
Working: Industry–construction 38% × 9% = 3.42; services 42% × 7% = 2.94; agriculture–forestry–fisheries 12% × 3% = 0.36; product taxes less subsidies 8% × 6% = 0.48; total = 3.42 + 2.94 + 0.36 + 0.48 = 7.2%.
Check: Shares 38 + 42 + 12 + 8 = 100% ✓.
Analysis: Industry–construction contributes 47.5% and services 40.8% of growth.

APE-007.q: Labour moving from agriculture to industry and services raises economy-wide productivity mainly through:
APE-007.e: As this room narrows, productivity growth must come within sectors (technology, management).
o: The structural change effect – workers move to higher-productivity sectors
APE-007.x:
Basis: Development economics (Lewis 1954 – dual-sector model; McMillan & Rodrik 2011 – structural change).
Analysis: Farm labour productivity is far below modern industry and services → moving workers raises aggregate productivity even with unchanged sector productivity (the structural 'between' effect). As the farm labour share falls, this room shrinks → productivity must come from 'within' sectors (technology, management).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the mechanism.

APE-008.q: Select ALL quality medium-term growth drivers for an economy like Vietnam:
APE-008.e: Prolonged negative real rates cause inflation, asset bubbles and misallocation.
o: High-tech FDI with stronger links to local firms
Institutional reform and private sector development
Prolonged negative real interest rates to boost demand
APE-008.x:
Basis: Development economics; World Bank Vietnam 2045 report.
Analysis: Quality drivers: (A) efficient public infrastructure – lower logistics costs, higher potential (MCR-060); (B) high-tech FDI linked to local firms – spillovers (APE-070); (C) institutional reform and private-sector development (ADE-081); (D) digitalisation and labour productivity (MCR-091).
Distractors: (E) Prolonged negative real rates cause inflation, asset bubbles and misallocation – unsustainable growth.

APE-009.q: As the 'demographic dividend' fades and the population ages, long-run growth depends more on:
APE-009.e: With labour no longer growing fast, productivity is the main driver.
o: Labour productivity and human capital quality
APE-009.x:
Basis: Development economics (Bloom & Williamson 1998 – demographic dividend); UNFPA (Vietnam's 'golden population' since 2007, expected to last to about 2039).
Analysis: The golden period: a high working-age share → a demographic dividend (abundant labour and saving). As it narrows and ageing sets in: slower labour growth, rising dependency → growth must rely on labour productivity and human capital (ADE-082).
Distractors: B – unskilled labour no longer grows fast; C and D are unsustainable.
Note (long-term investing): ageing creates opportunities in healthcare, insurance, asset management, and challenges for cheap-labour industries.

APE-010.q: Retail sales published at current prices include price effects; assessing real consumption requires removing inflation.
APE-010.e: True. Compare nominal growth with CPI to estimate real growth.
APE-010.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; the statistics office's trade statistics.
Analysis: True. Total retail sales of goods and consumer services are reported at current (nominal) prices, including price effects. For real consumption, strip out inflation (APE-011) or use constant-price data (the statistics office also reports growth 'excluding price factors').

APE-011.q: Nominal retail sales rise 9% and CPI 3.5%. What is approximate real growth (exact, %, 2 decimals)?
APE-011.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (Fisher relation).
Working: Real growth = 1.09 / 1.035 − 1 = 1.05314 − 1 ≈ 5.31% (approximation: 9 − 3.5 = 5.5%).
Analysis: Use a matching retail price index (goods/services CPI) rather than headline CPI where available. Real retail growth is a key domestic-demand gauge for retail and consumer stocks.

APE-012.q: A sharp acceleration in public investment disbursement first and most directly affects:
APE-012.e: Spillovers later reach jobs, consumption and long-run capacity.
o: Infrastructure contractors and building materials (steel, cement, aggregates, asphalt)
APE-012.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; Public Investment Law 2024.
Analysis: Faster public investment disbursement hits infrastructure contractors (bridges, roads, expressways) and building materials (steel, cement, aggregates, asphalt) earliest and most directly – via construction volume. Spillovers follow: jobs, consumption, long-run capacity.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't directly linked.
Note (investing): check contract backlog, financial capacity (working capital, debt) and the sector's typically thin margins before expecting gains.

APE-013.e: Household business tax reforms (e-invoices, declarations) aim to shrink it.
o: A narrow tax base, statistics that may understate the economy, and workers lacking social protection
APE-013.x:
Basis: Development economics (Schneider & Enste 2000; ILO – informal economy).
Analysis: A large informal sector: a narrow tax base (low revenue relative to the economy), statistics that may understate output, workers without contracts or social insurance; low productivity and poor credit access. E-invoicing and ending presumptive tax for household businesses (from 2026 under new rules – check the texts) aim to formalise it.
Distractors: B, C and D say the opposite.

APE-014.q: Remittances are USD 15 billion and GDP 480 billion. What share of GDP is that (%, 2 decimals)?
APE-014.e: 15/480 ≈ 3.13% of GDP – an important FX supply supporting the currency.
APE-014.x:
Basis: IMF BPM6 (secondary income); Vietnam remittance data.
Working: Remittances/GDP = 15 / 480 = 3.125% ≈ 3.13% of GDP.
Analysis: Remittances are a steady FX source (less cyclical than portfolio flows), supporting the currency, reserves and the current account (MCR-084). Part flows into property and deposits.

APE-015.q: A high investment/GDP ratio doesn't guarantee high growth if investment efficiency is low (high ICOR).
APE-015.e: True. Allocation quality matters more than volume.
APE-015.x:
Basis: Development economics (ICOR – MCR-099, MCR-100).
Analysis: True. Growth ≈ (I/Y) / ICOR: high investment/GDP with a high ICOR (inefficient investment – delayed, scattered projects, weak SOEs) still yields low growth. Allocation quality matters more than scale.
Note (companies): likewise, heavy capex with low ROIC creates no value (BAN-047).

APE-016.q: Real estate has large economy-wide spillovers mainly through:
APE-016.e: Property is common collateral, so price falls hit credit quality.
o: Bank credit, building materials and construction, and wealth effects on consumption
APE-016.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; IMF Global Financial Stability Report (real estate–finance links).
Analysis: Real estate spills over via: (1) bank credit – a large property loan share and property as common collateral → falling prices raise NPLs and cut borrowing capacity; (2) materials, construction and furnishing; (3) wealth effects on consumption; (4) the corporate bond market (Vietnam 2022–2023).
Distractors: B, C and D are incomplete or wrong.
Note (bank analysis): assess property-loan share, collateral and corporate bonds held by CTG, BID, VCB… when the property cycle turns down.

APE-017.q: Under the 2010 Law on the State Bank of Vietnam, the SBV is:
APE-017.e: It manages money, banking and FX and performs central bank functions.
o: A ministerial-level agency of the Government and the central bank
A body under the National Assembly
APE-017.x:
Basis: Law on the State Bank of Vietnam No. 46/2010/QH12 Art. 2.
Analysis: The SBV is a ministry-level Government agency and the central bank of Vietnam; it manages money, banking and FX and performs central-bank functions (issuing currency, banker to credit institutions, monetary services to the Government). As a Government body, it's less independent than many central banks (MCR-040).
Distractors: B, C and D misstate its legal status.
Note: Check for any current amendments to the SBV Law.

APE-018.q: Vietnam's central exchange rate mechanism (since 2016) features:
APE-018.e: It's a managed float; the band can be adjusted over time.
o: The SBV sets a daily central rate based on market developments, a currency basket and macro balances; banks trade within a band around it
Each bank sets rates without limits
APE-018.x:
Basis: Decision 2730/QD-NHNN (31 Dec 2015) – central rate mechanism from 4 Jan 2016; the band widened from ±3% to ±5% on 17 Oct 2022.
Analysis: The SBV publishes a daily VND/USD central rate based on: average interbank rates, movements of a basket of 8 major trading-partner currencies, and macro balances; banks trade within a band around it → a managed float.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: Band and method may change – check current rules.

APE-019.q: The central rate is VND 24,000/USD with a ±5% band. What is the ceiling rate banks may trade at?
APE-019.x:
Basis: Central rate mechanism (APE-018).
Working: Ceiling = 24,000 × (1 + 5%) = 25,200 VND/USD; floor = 24,000 × 0.95 = 22,800.
Analysis: When market rates near the ceiling, the SBV usually intervenes (selling FX – often at an intervention price below the ceiling), raises VND rates and drains liquidity (APE-027).

APE-020.q: Overnight interbank rates spike for a few days, especially at quarter-end. The most reasonable reading:
APE-020.e: Watch open market operations, bills and the exchange rate to see if it's temporary or a trend.
o: Temporarily tight system liquidity (higher short-term demand, seasonality or central bank absorption)
APE-020.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics (interbank market).
Analysis: Overnight rates spiking for days, especially at quarter-end → temporary system liquidity strain: higher short-term needs (banks meeting period-end ratios, Tet withdrawals, tax payments), or central bank draining via bills or FX sales (absorbing VND). Watch OMO, bills and FX to tell temporary from a tightening trend.
Distractors: B, C and D jump to conclusions.
Note: One short-lived signal isn't enough to change a cycle view – avoid overreaction.

APE-021.q: Select ALL signals to watch when assessing the monetary policy stance:
APE-021.e: Gold prices are affected by policy, not an interest rate tool.
o: Net injection/withdrawal via open market operations
Gold bar prices as an interest rate tool
APE-021.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics; SBV Law 2010 Art. 10.
Analysis: Signals of monetary stance: (A) net OMO injections/withdrawals; (B) SBV bill issuance (draining liquidity); (C) policy rates (refinancing, rediscount, OMO); (D) interbank rates and credit growth (quotas).
Distractors: (E) Gold prices are a market affected by policy, not a rate-setting tool.
Note (FERGASITOR): these are macro–liquidity indicators for a weekly dashboard (MCR-044, APE-098).

APE-022.q: System credit is 13,500 at the start and 15,120 at year-end (VND trillion). What is credit growth (%)?
APE-022.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics.
Working: Credit growth = 15,120 / 13,500 − 1 = 1.12 − 1 = 12%.
Analysis: Versus nominal GDP growth (say 10%) → credit outpaces GDP → credit/GDP keeps rising (APE-023, APE-024). Credit growth is a key liquidity gauge for stocks and bank earnings.
Check: 13,500 × 1.12 = 15,120 ✓.

APE-023.q: Credit is VND 15,120 trillion and nominal GDP 12,000 trillion. What is credit/GDP (%)?
APE-023.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics; BIS (credit-to-GDP).
Working: Credit/GDP = 15,120 / 12,000 = 1.26 = 126%.
Analysis: 126% is high for developing economies at similar income (often 50–100%) → heavy reliance on bank funding and risk concentrated in banks; capital markets (bonds, equities) need developing.
Check: 12,000 × 1.26 = 15,120 ✓.

APE-024.q: An already high credit/GDP ratio rising faster than nominal GDP for years increases financial stability risk.
APE-024.e: True. The 'credit-to-GDP gap' is a BIS early-warning indicator of banking crises.
APE-024.x:
Basis: BIS – Basel III (credit-to-GDP gap, the basis for countercyclical capital buffers); Borio & Lowe (2002).
Analysis: True. High credit/GDP rising faster than nominal GDP for years → rising economy-wide leverage, weaker debt service capacity and bubble formation → financial-stability risk. The BIS uses the credit-to-GDP gap versus its long-run trend (> 10 points) as an early-warning indicator of banking crises.

APE-025.q: Banks raise deposit rates en masse as credit outpaces deposits. The likely next effect:
APE-025.e: Highly leveraged firms and real estate are most sensitive.
o: Lending rates follow, raising firms' funding costs
APE-025.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics (bank rate transmission).
Analysis: Credit outpacing deposits → funding shortfalls and a deposit-rate race → higher funding costs → lending rates rise (to protect NIM) → higher borrowing costs for firms; leveraged firms and property suffer most (the reverse of APE-037).
Distractors: B, C and D have the wrong direction.
Note (bank analysis): banks with high CASA face less funding-cost pressure – steadier NIM.

APE-026.q: A bank has loans of 900 and customer deposits of 1,000. What is the simple loan-to-deposit ratio (%)?
APE-026.e: 900/1,000 = 90%; a high LDR limits credit growth room without more deposits.
APE-026.x:
Basis: Bank analysis; Circular 22/2019/TT-NHNN (loan-to-deposit ratio – max 85% for commercial banks, with its own formula).
Working: Simple LDR = 900 / 1,000 = 90%.
Analysis: A high LDR → limited room to grow credit without more deposits; higher liquidity risk. The regulatory LDR uses its own adjustments – don't compare the simple figure directly with the 85% cap.

APE-027.q: The Fed hikes sharply and the USD strengthens globally. Typical pressure on the VND and possible policy responses:
APE-027.e: There's a trade-off between FX stability and supporting growth.
o: VND depreciation pressure; the central bank may sell FX, absorb VND liquidity or raise rates
The central bank must cut rates
APE-027.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics (MCR-036, MCR-080); SBV practice in 2022 and 2024.
Analysis: Aggressive Fed hikes and a strong USD → a narrower VND–USD rate gap, capital outflows, depreciation pressure. The SBV may sell reserves, drain VND liquidity (bills) and raise policy rates (as in 2022) → trading exchange-rate stability against growth support.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

APE-028.q: A firm borrows USD at 6% instead of VND at 9%, unhedged. The VND depreciates 4% against USD in the year. What is the effective VND cost (%, 2 decimals)?
APE-028.e: 1.06 × 1.04 − 1 = 10.24% > 9%: the 'cheap' USD loan turns out dearer.
APE-028.x:
Basis: International finance (FX borrowing cost in local terms – uncovered interest parity).
Working: Effective VND cost = (1 + 6%) × (1 + 4%) − 1 = 1.06 × 1.04 − 1 = 1.1024 − 1 = 10.24% > 9% for VND.
Analysis: The USD rate is 3 points 'cheaper', but a 4% VND fall makes it 1.24 points dearer than VND. Break-even depreciation = 1.09/1.06 − 1 ≈ 2.83%. Firms without USD revenue bear big risk (APE-029).
Check: Borrow USD 1,000 → repay USD 1,060 × a 4% higher rate = 1,102.4 (in original VND terms) ✓.

APE-029.q: An unhedged foreign-currency loan may look cheaper on interest but carries exchange rate risk.
APE-029.e: True. Firms without FX revenue are most exposed.
APE-029.x:
Basis: International finance (FX risk – VAS 10, IFRS 7).
Analysis: True. Unhedged FX borrowing: a lower nominal rate but exchange-rate risk – local-currency depreciation raises debt service in local terms and creates remeasurement losses (CAS-037). Firms without FX revenue (no natural hedge) are most exposed.
Note (equity analysis): check disclosures on FX debt, USD revenue and hedges (power, airlines, steelmakers importing inputs).

APE-030.q: Growth is slowing but the VND faces depreciation pressure. A central bank wanting to cut rates faces difficulty because:
APE-030.e: It's the impossible trinity in practice; liquidity and targeted credit tools are often added.
o: Cutting narrows the VND–USD rate gap, adding FX pressure and capital outflows
APE-030.x:
Basis: International macroeconomics (the trilemma – MCR-080).
Analysis: Cutting rates to support growth → a narrower VND–USD gap → less attractive VND assets, outflows, FX speculation → more depreciation pressure → conflicting goals. In practice the SBV combines flexible liquidity tools, targeted credit and FX intervention rather than relying on rates alone.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

APE-031.q: A large, persistent premium of domestic gold prices over converted world prices usually reflects:
APE-031.e: Wide gaps encourage smuggling, affecting the FX market.
o: Supply restrictions (imports, bar production) against high hoarding demand; it can pressure FX via informal channels
APE-031.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics; Decree 24/2012/ND-CP on gold trading (amended – check current text).
Analysis: A persistent large domestic–world gold premium reflects restricted supply (SBV monopoly on gold bars, limited raw-gold imports) amid strong hoarding demand → incentives to smuggle gold and buy FX informally → FX pressure. In 2024 the SBV sold gold bars to narrow the gap.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: Gold-market rules may have been amended after 2024.

APE-032.q: Select ALL signs of stress at a commercial bank:
APE-032.e: Rising CASA is usually positive (cheaper funding).
o: Rapidly rising NPLs and special-mention (group 2) loans
Deposit outflows with unusually high deposit rates
Heavy reliance on short-term interbank funding
APE-032.x:
Basis: Bank analysis (CAMELS); Circular 11/2021/TT-NHNN (loan classification).
Analysis: Stress signs: (A) fast-rising NPLs (groups 3–5) and group-2 loans (special mention – an early indicator); (B) falling NPL coverage – a thin buffer (APE-033); (C) shrinking deposits and unusually high deposit rates – lost confidence, liquidity shortage; (D) reliance on short-term interbank funding – unstable funding.
Distractors: (E) Rising CASA is usually positive (cheap funding, sticky customers).
Note: Priority metrics when analysing CTG, BID and VCB under the bank-analysis principles.

APE-033.q: A bank has loan loss provisions of 150 and NPLs of 120. What is NPL coverage (%)?
APE-033.x:
Basis: Bank analysis (NPL coverage – LLR).
Working: Coverage = credit loss provisions / NPLs = 150 / 120 = 125%.
Analysis: Provisions exceed NPLs by 25% → a decent loss-absorbing buffer, with room for provision write-backs to support profit as NPLs fall. Review alongside NPL quality (collateral), group-2 loans, restructured loans and corporate bonds.

APE-034.q: When the central bank cuts policy rates, commercial lending rates fall immediately and fully.
APE-034.e: False. Transmission is lagged and partial, depending on funding costs, credit risk and competition.
APE-034.x:
Basis: Applied monetary economics (interest rate pass-through – IMF 2012).
Analysis: False. Pass-through from policy to lending rates is lagged (months) and incomplete: it depends on funding costs (older high-rate term deposits), credit risk (high NPLs keep spreads wide), competition, credit demand and maturity structure. In Vietnam, lending rates usually fall more slowly than deposit rates.

APE-035.q: In the 'investment clock' (growth–inflation), the recovery phase (rising growth, low inflation) usually favours:
APE-035.e: Overheat: commodities; stagflation: cash; recession: bonds. It's a reference frame, not a hard rule.
APE-035.x:
Basis: Merrill Lynch (2004) – 'The Investment Clock'; cycle–asset frameworks.
Analysis: Recovery (rising growth, low inflation): earnings rebound strongly while rates stay low → equities usually do best. Overheat: commodities; stagflation: cash; reflation/recession: bonds (APE-036).
Distractors: B, C and D belong to other phases.
Note: A guide, not a rigid law – combine with actual valuation (FERGASITOR: Cycle → Valuation → TA).

APE-036.q: Match each cycle phase (investment clock) with the asset class usually favoured:
APE-036.e: Use it for orientation, combined with actual valuations.
APE-036.x:
Basis: Merrill Lynch – The Investment Clock.
Analysis: Recession (falling growth and inflation) → central banks ease, rates fall → bonds rally. Recovery (rising growth, low inflation) → equities. Overheat (high growth, rising inflation) → commodities. Stagflation (falling growth, high inflation) → cash and short-term assets (high rates hurt both stocks and bonds).
Note: Real cycles don't always follow this order and vary in length; starting valuations drive returns more than cycle phase.

APE-037.q: When the cycle turns to monetary easing (falling rates), the earliest beneficiaries are usually:
APE-037.e: Funding costs fall and asset valuations rise.
o: Rate-sensitive firms: real estate, brokers, highly leveraged companies
APE-037.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (interest-rate and asset-price channels – MCR-038).
Analysis: Monetary easing and lower rates → rate-sensitive groups gain first: property (lower funding costs for developers and buyers, better liquidity), brokers (brokerage, margin lending and proprietary income rise with active markets), leveraged firms (lower interest, profits jump via financial leverage); asset values rise on lower discount rates.
Distractors: B, C and D gain little or lose (cash-rich firms earn less interest).

APE-038.q: The market P/E is 12 (earnings yield E/P); the 10-year government bond yields 4%. What is the simple equity risk premium proxy (E/P − bond yield, pp, 2 decimals)?
APE-038.e: E/P = 1/12 ≈ 8.33%; 8.33 − 4 = 4.33 points. A crude measure ignoring earnings growth.
APE-038.x:
Basis: Market valuation (Fed model – Yardeni 1997; equity risk premium).
Working: E/P = 1/12 ≈ 8.33%; premium = 8.33% − 4% ≈ 4.33 points.
Analysis: A high positive premium → equities look attractive versus bonds. A crude gauge: it compares a quasi-real equity yield (E/P, with inflation-linked growth) with a nominal bond yield, ignoring earnings growth, quality and risk. Watch the trend, not a point.
Note: Versus the current system's Ke of 12.63%: an E/P of 8.33% is below Ke → meaningful earnings growth is needed to justify P/E 12.

APE-039.q: Stock markets often lead the real economy by several months because they price expectations.
APE-039.e: True. By the time data confirm, prices have usually moved.
APE-039.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; Conference Board (stocks are an LEI component – MCR-068).
Analysis: True. Share prices reflect expected earnings and rates (ADE-017) → they usually lead the real economy by months (bottoming before the worst data, peaking before growth slows). Waiting for economic confirmation often means prices have moved most of the way.
Note: Markets also give false signals (Samuelson: 'predicted nine of the last five recessions') – combine technical confirmation (monthly/weekly MACD) with valuation.

APE-040.q: Property credit tightens while projects face prolonged legal hold-ups. The biggest risk for highly leveraged developers is:
APE-040.e: Sales cash flow is blocked while debt obligations still fall due.
o: Liquidity shortfalls and inability to repay maturing loans and bonds
APE-040.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; VSA 570 (CAS-060).
Analysis: Tight property credit + long legal delays → no sales launches, blocked sales cash, no new loans, while loan and bond maturities keep coming → liquidity shortfall and default risk (Vietnam 2022–2023: many developers missed bond payments).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (investment risk): first check developers' 12-month maturities, cash and operating cash flow – survival before growth.

APE-041.q: The deposit rate is 5% and inflation 3.5%. What is the real deposit return (exact, %, 2 decimals)?
APE-041.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (Fisher relation).
Working: Real yield = 1.05 / 1.035 − 1 = 1.014493 − 1 ≈ 1.45% (approximation 5 − 3.5 = 1.5%).
Analysis: A positive but low real deposit yield → low opportunity cost of cash, pushing money toward higher-yielding assets (stocks, property). It's the floor for judging investments: risk-adjusted expected returns must clear it comfortably (Ke of 12.63% already includes a risk premium).

APE-042.q: A steelmaker's margin is driven most by:
APE-042.e: It's cyclical; valuation should use normalised through-cycle earnings.
o: The spread between finished steel and raw materials (ore, coking coal, scrap) – often moved by construction demand and big producers' policies
APE-042.x:
Basis: Industry economics (steel spread – APE-052).
Analysis: Steel margins hinge on the product–raw-material spread (iron ore and coking coal for blast furnaces; scrap for EAFs): steel prices follow construction demand (property, public investment) and China's export policy (over 50% of world output); input prices follow Australia and Brazil. High-cost raw-material stock during steel price falls causes inventory losses.
Distractors: B, C and D have small effects.
Note: A cyclical sector – value on normalised earnings (APE-050) and track the spread weekly.

APE-043.q: Select ALL warning signs of an asset bubble:
APE-043.e: Rental yields rising faster than prices mean valuations are becoming more attractive.
o: Very fast credit growth into the sector
Prices far outpacing incomes and rents
A spreading 'this time is different' narrative
Rental yields rising faster than prices
APE-043.x:
Basis: Kindleberger – Manias, Panics, and Crashes; Minsky (1986); Reinhart & Rogoff (2009) – This Time Is Different.
Analysis: Bubble signs: (A) very fast credit growth into the sector; (B) prices far outrunning incomes and rents (falling rental yields – APE-044, APE-045); (C) widespread leveraged speculation and flipping; (D) spreading 'this time is different' narratives.
Distractors: (E) Rents rising faster than prices → valuations becoming more attractive, the opposite of a bubble.
Note (psychology): peak FOMO often coincides with a bubble's late stage.

APE-044.q: An apartment costing VND 6 billion rents for 15 million/month. What is the gross annual rental yield (%)?
APE-044.x:
Basis: Financial economics (gross rental yield).
Working: Gross yield = 15 × 12 / 6,000 = 180 / 6,000 = 3% a year.
Analysis: The net yield is lower (after management, maintenance, tax, vacancy – often 2–2.5%). The property's 'P/E' ≈ 33× (6,000 / 180) → high, and below deposit rates (APE-045).

APE-045.q: Rental yields persistently below deposit rates show property prices rely heavily on capital-gain expectations.
APE-045.e: True. When expectations reverse, prices can correct sharply.
APE-045.x:
Basis: Financial economics (Shiller; cash-flow-based property valuation).
Analysis: True. Rental yields persistently below deposit rates → investors accept low cash flow because they expect capital gains → prices rest on expectations, not cash flow → when expectations turn (rate hikes, credit tightening), prices can fall sharply and liquidity dries up.

APE-046.q: A steepening yield curve (long yields rising faster than short) usually reflects:
APE-046.e: Check the cause (growth vs fiscal risk) to read it correctly.
o: Rising expected growth or inflation, or a higher term premium
The central bank directly cutting long rates
APE-046.x:
Basis: Financial economics (expectations theory and the term premium).
Analysis: A steepening curve (bear or bull steepening): rising expected growth/inflation (future hikes), or a higher term premium (fiscal risk, heavy long-bond supply, inflation uncertainty). Distinguish the cause: growth optimism (good for equities) versus fiscal worries (bad).
Distractors: B – inversion, not steepening, signals recession (MCR-071); C is the opposite; D – central banks mainly steer short rates.

APE-047.q: A bond has modified duration 5. Market yields rise 1 point. By roughly how much does its price change (%)?
APE-047.x:
Basis: Financial economics (modified duration – Macaulay 1938; Hicks 1939).
Working: ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod × Δy = −5 × 1% = −5%.
Analysis: Duration measures bond price sensitivity to rates; actual falls are slightly smaller due to convexity. The same logic applies to growth stocks – long 'duration' (value in distant cash flows) → more rate-sensitive than value stocks (APE-099).

APE-048.q: Securities margin debt surging to record highs usually:
APE-048.e: Track margin/market cap as a systemic risk indicator.
o: Amplifies volatility: when prices fall, cascading forced selling deepens declines
APE-048.x:
Basis: Financial economics (Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009 – liquidity and margin spirals).
Analysis: Record margin debt amplifies volatility: as prices fall, accounts hit thresholds → forced selling → further declines → more liquidations → a cascade (Vietnam 2018, 2022). On the way up, margin pushes prices up fast.
Distractors: B, C and D say the opposite.
Note (personal risk management): keep a personal margin cap and cut leverage first when trend signals weaken (weekly MACD, VNI) – avoiding system-wide liquidation spirals.

APE-049.q: Stock market liquidity is unrelated to monetary conditions.
APE-049.e: False. Rates, system liquidity and credit strongly affect flows into stocks.
APE-049.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (liquidity and asset prices – Adrian & Shin 2010).
Analysis: False. Interest rates (opportunity and margin costs), bank liquidity (OMO, interbank), credit and M2 growth strongly drive money into stocks. In Vietnam, low rates and ample liquidity in 2020–2021 brought record turnover; tightening in 2022 cut it sharply.

APE-050.q: A cyclical stock has a very low P/E with earnings at the cycle peak. The right approach:
APE-050.e: For cyclicals, P/E is usually highest at the trough and lowest at the earnings peak.
o: Value it on normalised through-cycle earnings; a low P/E at the peak can be a value trap
Buy now because P/E is low
APE-050.x:
Basis: Valuation (Graham & Dodd – normalised earnings; Damodaran – cyclical firms).
Analysis: Cyclicals earn peak profits in boom phases → very low P/E at the top (high earnings, price not yet reflecting the coming decline) and very high P/E at the bottom (low or negative earnings) → a paradox. The right approach: value on normalised through-cycle earnings (multi-year average EPS or margins), P/B, EV/capacity; a low P/E at the peak can be a value trap.
Distractors: B and C apply P/E mechanically; D ignores the cycle.

APE-051.q: The 'China + 1' supply chain shift most clearly benefits:
APE-051.e: Gains depend on infrastructure, energy, skilled labour and origin rules.
o: Industrial parks, logistics, supporting manufacturers and factory labour
APE-051.x:
Basis: Applied international economics ('China + 1'; UNCTAD World Investment Report).
Analysis: Multinationals diversifying production beyond China → manufacturing FDI into Vietnam → clearest gains for: industrial parks (land and factory leasing), logistics (ports, warehousing, transport), supporting industries (components, packaging) and factory labour. Gains depend on infrastructure, reliable power, skilled labour and rules of origin (transshipment risk – APE-071).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't directly linked.
Note (sector investing): track registered vs disbursed FDI, occupancy and industrial land rents.

APE-052.q: Hot-rolled coil is USD 600/t. Each tonne needs 1.6 t of ore (USD 110/t) and 0.8 t of coking coal (USD 250/t). What is the steel–raw material spread (USD/t)?
APE-052.x:
Basis: Industry economics (blast-furnace steel spread).
Working: Raw materials = 1.6 × 110 + 0.8 × 250 = 176 + 200 = USD 376/tonne; spread = 600 − 376 = USD 224/tonne.
Analysis: The 224 spread must cover conversion costs (energy, labour, depreciation, interest) – at about 150/tonne, the margin is about 74/tonne. A 10% steel price drop (60) cuts the spread 27% → very high profit sensitivity (operating leverage – BAN-063).
Check: 376 + 224 = 600 ✓.

APE-053.q: The 'bullwhip effect' in supply chains is when:
APE-053.e: Caused by order-based forecasting, batch ordering and hoarding in shortages.
o: Small swings in final demand amplify into bigger swings in upstream orders
APE-053.x:
Basis: Lee, Padmanabhan & Whang (1997), 'The Bullwhip Effect in Supply Chains'; Forrester (1961).
Analysis: The bullwhip effect: small swings in final demand become larger swings in upstream orders (retail → distribution → manufacturing → materials). Causes: forecasting from orders rather than true demand, batch ordering, price/promotion swings, hoarding during shortages. Example: the 2021–2023 chip cycle.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note (investing): upstream firms (materials, components) have more volatile revenue and profit than retailers.

APE-054.q: Highly concentrated industries (dominated by few firms) usually have more pricing power.
APE-054.e: True, though it also depends on entry barriers, substitutes and regulation.
APE-054.x:
Basis: Industrial organisation (structure–conduct–performance, Bain 1951).
Analysis: True (conditionally). Highly concentrated industries (a few dominant firms) → easier tacit coordination (MIC-082) and more pricing power. But entry barriers (low barriers invite entry), substitutes, buyer power and regulation (state-set prices) also matter.
Note: Combine HHI (APE-055) with Porter's five forces (BAN-092).

APE-055.q: Four firms hold market shares of 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. What is the HHI?
APE-055.x:
Basis: Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (Hirschman 1945; Herfindahl 1950).
Working: HHI = Σ(share %)² = 40² + 30² + 20² + 10² = 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000.
Analysis: HHI runs from near 0 (perfect competition) to 10,000 (monopoly). Squaring weights large firms more – capturing dominance better than the CR4 ratio (here CR4 = 100%).

APE-056.q: An HHI of 3,000 is usually classed as:
APE-056.e: Competition authorities use HHI levels and changes to screen mergers.
APE-056.x:
Basis: US DOJ/FTC Horizontal Merger Guidelines (2010: > 2,500 highly concentrated; 2023: > 1,800); Decree 35/2020/ND-CP under the Competition Law 2018 (HHI for economic concentration reviews).
Analysis: HHI = 3,000 exceeds 2,500 (2010 Guidelines) → highly concentrated; also under the 2023 threshold of 1,800. Competition authorities screen deals using post-deal HHI and ΔHHI for possible restriction of competition.
Distractors: B and C are wrong; D – pure monopoly is 10,000.
Note: Vietnam's specific thresholds are in Decree 35/2020 – check the original text.

APE-057.q: Select ALL factors raising supplier bargaining power:
APE-057.x:
Basis: Porter (1979) – supplier bargaining power.
Analysis: Suppliers are powerful when: (A) few substitutes exist (more concentrated than buyers); (B) switching costs are high; (C) inputs are differentiated and critical to quality; (D) they can integrate forward (making the buyer's product). E.g., chips, premium iron ore, core software.
Distractors: (E) Many substitute suppliers reduce their power.

APE-058.q: Industrial electricity tariffs rise 5%. The most affected firms are:
APE-058.e: Margin impact depends on power's cost share and pass-through ability.
o: Energy-intensive industries: steel, cement, chemicals, yarn
APE-058.x:
Basis: Industry economics; MOIT/EVN retail electricity price adjustments (under Decision 05/2024/QD-TTg).
Analysis: A 5% industrial power price rise hits energy-intensive sectors hardest: steel (EAF), cement (grinding), chemicals (chlor-alkali, urea), yarn, paper – where power is a large cost share. Margin impact = power cost share × 5% × (1 − pass-through ability).
Distractors: B, C and D have small power cost shares.
Note: Check the current power-pricing mechanism.

APE-059.q: Container freight rises from USD 2,000 to 5,000 per 40-foot box; cargo value per box is USD 50,000. By how many points does freight's share of cargo value rise?
APE-059.e: From 4% to 10% → up 6 points; low-value goods (wood, farm produce) are hit harder.
APE-059.x:
Basis: Industry economics (logistics costs).
Working: Freight share before = 2,000 / 50,000 = 4%; after = 5,000 / 50,000 = 10%; up 10% − 4% = 6 points.
Analysis: Low-value-per-container goods (wood, farm products, materials – maybe USD 15,000–20,000 per box) suffer far more: the same 3,000 rise adds 15–20 points → possibly wiping out margins. Examples: the 2021 freight spike and the 2024 Red Sea crisis.

APE-060.q: Just-in-time inventory cuts working capital but makes firms more vulnerable to supply chain disruptions.
APE-060.e: True. Many firms moved to 'just-in-case' for critical items.
APE-060.x:
Basis: Supply chain management (Toyota Production System – Ohno 1988).
Analysis: True. Just-in-time cuts inventory → less working capital, storage cost and obsolescence; but with no buffer, disruptions (COVID-19, the 2021 chip shortage, disasters) halt production at once. Many firms moved to 'just-in-case' for critical items – trading cost for resilience (APE-064).
Note (financial analysis): faster inventory turnover (good for ROIC) may come with higher disruption risk.

APE-061.q: Which trade policy risk is specific to seafood exporters?
APE-061.e: Administrative review outcomes can swing profits sharply.
o: Anti-dumping and countervailing duties, technical and food-safety barriers in importing countries
APE-061.x:
Basis: WTO Anti-Dumping and SCM Agreements; US Department of Commerce (administrative reviews – PORs – on pangasius and shrimp).
Analysis: Seafood exporters face specific trade-policy risks: anti-dumping and countervailing duties (pangasius and shrimp into the US – review outcomes can swing duty rates and profits); technical and food-safety barriers (antibiotics, the US catfish inspection programme); the EU IUU 'yellow card' on wild catch.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't sector-specific risks.
Note (VHC, ANV…): track POR results, US reciprocal tariffs and raw fish prices.

APE-062.q: A garment maker moves from cut-make-trim (CMT) to FOB and ODM to:
APE-062.e: In exchange it needs more working capital and bears inventory and material price risk.
o: Capture more value added: sourcing materials, design, chain management, and better meeting origin rules
APE-062.x:
Basis: Textile industry economics (Gereffi 1999 – upgrading in global value chains).
Analysis: CMT (cut–make–trim): materials supplied by the buyer, earning only a processing fee (CAS-006). FOB: buying materials, managing production and delivery – more value added. ODM: own design. Upgrading raises value added and helps meet 'yarn-forward' origin rules (CPTPP – APE-068). In return: more working capital, inventory and raw-material price risk.
Distractors: B, C and D defeat the purpose.

APE-063.q: An electronics export shipment is worth 100 with 70 of imported components. What is the domestic value-added share (%)?
APE-063.e: (100 − 70)/100 = 30%: large export values don't necessarily mean much domestic value.
APE-063.x:
Basis: Applied international economics (OECD TiVA – trade in value added).
Working: Domestic value added = (100 − 70) / 100 = 30%.
Analysis: Exports of 100 contain only 30 of value created domestically (wages, profits, depreciation) – much of it possibly accruing to FDI firms. That's why high openness (APE-002) doesn't mean an equivalent GDP contribution, and why localisation targets matter.

APE-064.q: Select ALL measures that strengthen supply chain resilience:
APE-064.e: Single sourcing minimises cost in normal times but is risky under shocks.
APE-064.x:
Basis: Supply chain management (Sheffi 2005 – The Resilient Enterprise).
Analysis: Building resilience: (A) diversify suppliers and source markets; (B) safety stock for critical items (just-in-case – APE-060); (C) localise or bring supply closer (nearshoring); (D) monitor supplier risk – financial, geopolitical (ICA-018).
Distractors: (E) A single supplier minimises cost in normal times but is very risky under shocks.

APE-065.q: Under comparative advantage (Ricardo), a country should specialise in goods with:
APE-065.e: Trade is beneficial even if a country is less efficient at everything.
o: A lower opportunity cost than other countries
APE-065.x:
Basis: Ricardo (1817) – On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (comparative advantage).
Analysis: Countries should specialise in goods with lower opportunity cost than others (comparative advantage), not necessarily the lowest absolute cost (Adam Smith's absolute advantage). Trade benefits both sides even if one is less efficient at everything.
Distractors: B is absolute advantage; C and D aren't the criterion.

APE-066.q: A small country imports 50 units at a world price of 100 and levies a 10% tariff. What is tariff revenue?
APE-066.e: Domestic price 110; revenue = 10 × 50 = 500 (assuming 50 units imported after the tariff).
APE-066.x:
Basis: International economics (tariffs in a small country).
Working: Tax per unit = 100 × 10% = 10; domestic price = 110; revenue = 10 × 50 = 500 (assuming post-tariff imports of 50).
Analysis: A small country can't affect world prices → the whole tariff passes into domestic prices, borne by consumers. In practice imports fall after the tariff (more domestic output, less consumption) – revenue is on post-tariff imports (APE-067).

APE-067.q: Effects of an import tariff in a small country:
APE-067.e: The deadweight loss comprises production and consumption distortions.
o: Consumers lose surplus; domestic producers and the budget gain; society bears a deadweight loss
APE-067.x:
Basis: International economics (tariff welfare analysis – Krugman & Obstfeld).
Analysis: A small country's import tariff: higher domestic prices → consumers lose surplus (the biggest effect); domestic producers gain; the budget collects revenue; the net is a deadweight loss of production distortion (high-cost domestic output replacing cheap imports) and consumption distortion (valuable consumption forgone).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong (only large countries might improve their terms of trade).

APE-068.q: In free trade agreements, rules of origin determine whether goods qualify for preferential tariffs.
APE-068.e: True. E.g., 'yarn forward' rules for textiles in some FTAs.
APE-068.x:
Basis: Applied international economics; CPTPP (yarn-forward rule); EVFTA (fabric-forward); MOIT circulars on origin.
Analysis: True. Rules of origin determine whether goods have enough in-bloc content (tariff shift, regional value content, processing operations) to receive FTA preferential rates – preventing non-members routing goods via members. E.g., garments shipped to Canada or Mexico under CPTPP must use yarn made within the bloc.

APE-069.e: Conversely, 'trade creation' shifts to more efficient sources.
o: An FTA shifts imports from a more efficient outside supplier to a less efficient member thanks to tariff preferences
APE-069.x:
Basis: Viner (1950) – The Customs Union Issue.
Analysis: Trade diversion: FTA preferences for members → imports shift from more efficient non-member suppliers (taxed) to less efficient members (duty-free) → welfare falls (lost tariff revenue, higher real cost). Trade creation: shifting from high-cost domestic output to imports from more efficient members → welfare rises. An FTA nets gains when creation exceeds diversion.
Distractors: B is trade creation; C and D are wrong.

APE-070.q: Select ALL benefits FDI can bring to a host country:
APE-070.e: Spillovers aren't automatic; they depend on local firms' absorptive capacity and linkages.
o: Technology and management spillovers (with local linkages)
Automatic full technology transfer in all cases
APE-070.x:
Basis: Development economics (Javorcik 2004 – FDI spillovers via backward linkages; UNCTAD).
Analysis: FDI benefits: (A) extra investment capital (MCR-087 – financing S − I gaps); (B) technology and management spillovers – if linked to local firms (suppliers, partners, job movers); (C) jobs; (D) export market access (corporate networks).
Distractors: (E) Spillovers aren't automatic – they depend on local absorptive capacity and linkages; many FDI firms in Vietnam operate as enclaves importing most inputs (APE-063).

APE-071.q: As trade tensions rise, importers tighten checks on illegal transhipment (origin fraud). Exporters should:
APE-071.e: Violations can bring very high duties and lost markets.
o: Prove origin clearly: materials records, production process, local value share
APE-071.x:
Basis: Applied international economics; Foreign Trade Management Law 2017; MOIT rules on anti-circumvention and origin fraud.
Analysis: When importers (e.g., the US) crack down on illegal transshipment, exporters must prove origin clearly: raw-material sourcing records, real production processes, domestic value content and tariff shifts. Violations can bring very high duties (anti-circumvention, transshipment tariffs), lost markets and industry-wide damage.
Distractors: B, C and D worsen the risk and may be unlawful.

APE-072.q: Final good tariff 20%; inputs are 50% of the final good's world value with a 10% tariff. What is the effective rate of protection (%)?
APE-072.x:
Basis: Corden (1966), 'The Structure of a Tariff System and the Effective Protective Rate'.
Working: ERP = (t_final − a × t_input) / (1 − a) = (0.20 − 0.5 × 0.10) / (1 − 0.5) = (0.20 − 0.05) / 0.5 = 0.15 / 0.5 = 30%.
Analysis: Effective protection measures how much tariffs raise domestic value added: a 20% nominal tariff on the final good protects value added by 30% because inputs are taxed less. Check: value added at world prices = 100 − 50 = 50; domestically = 120 − 55 = 65; (65 − 50)/50 = 30% ✓.

APE-073.q: Domestic currency depreciation can partly offset tariffs imposed by an importing country on exports.
APE-073.e: True, but it raises imported input costs and may be viewed as currency manipulation.
APE-073.x:
Basis: International economics (Lerner symmetry; exchange-rate pass-through).
Analysis: True. Depreciation makes exports cheaper in foreign currency → partly offsetting the importer's tariff. But it raises imported input costs (limited offset for processing economies – MCR-083), inflation and FX debt burdens (MCR-085), and partners may label it currency manipulation (monitored by the US Treasury).

APE-074.q: A major export market imposes high reciprocal tariffs. A sensible exporter response:
APE-074.e: Build tariff scenarios into financial planning.
o: Diversify markets, raise local content, negotiate cost-sharing with buyers, reassess the supply chain
APE-074.x:
Basis: Applied international economics; scenario analysis (BAN-058).
Analysis: Strategic responses to high reciprocal tariffs in a key market: diversify markets (EU, Japan via FTAs); raise local content and origin transparency (APE-071); negotiate tariff cost sharing with customers (APE-075); reassess supply chains; plan finances by tariff scenario (cash flow, working capital).
Distractors: B and C are extreme and value-destroying; D ignores the risk.
Note (investing): for exporters dependent on the US, assess revenue share, pass-through ability and position versus competitors facing different rates.

APE-075.q: An export priced at USD 100 FOB faces a 20% tariff abroad. After negotiation, the exporter bears 25% of the tariff via a price cut. What is the new FOB price (USD)?
APE-075.e: Tariff USD 20; exporter bears 25% = USD 5 → FOB 95.
APE-075.x:
Basis: International economics (tariff incidence – MIC-014, MIC-015).
Working: Tariff = 100 × 20% = USD 20; the exporter bears 25% = USD 5 (a FOB cut) → new FOB price = 100 − 5 = USD 95.
Analysis: The importer bears 75% = USD 15 (landed cost ≈ 95 × 1.2 = 114 versus 120 without the cut – the gap because duty is on the new FOB: 95 × 20% = 19, total 114). The split depends on relative elasticities and bargaining power.
Note: The question simplifies by taxing the original price; in practice duty applies to the new price.

APE-076.q: How does the 15% global minimum tax affect developing countries' FDI incentives?
APE-076.e: Top-up tax may be collected elsewhere unless the host applies a domestic minimum top-up tax.
o: CIT holidays lose appeal for large groups; many countries shift to non-tax support (infrastructure, training, investment cost support)
APE-076.x:
Basis: OECD Pillar Two (GloBE Rules, 2021); Resolution 107/2023/QH15 (global minimum tax top-up in Vietnam from 2024).
Analysis: A 15% global minimum tax for groups with revenue ≥ EUR 750 million: if a host's incentives push the effective rate below 15%, the gap is collected (by the parent country via IIR or the host via QDMTT) → CIT holidays lose appeal. Many countries (Vietnam – the Investment Support Fund under Decree 182/2024/ND-CP) shift to non-tax support: investment cost, training, R&D, infrastructure.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: Check current implementing guidance.

APE-077.q: A trade surplus always proves the economy is strong.
APE-077.e: False. It may stem from weak domestic demand cutting imports; examine components and causes.
APE-077.x:
Basis: Macroeconomics (CA = S − I; Krugman – the 'competitiveness' fallacy).
Analysis: False. A trade surplus may reflect weak domestic demand (falling consumption and investment cutting imports of machinery and materials – a sign of slower future output), not competitiveness. Look at components: rising exports (positive) versus falling imports (possibly negative – APE-091); which sector drives it (FDI or domestic – APE-003).

APE-078.q: The gravity model predicts bilateral trade:
APE-078.e: FTAs, shared borders and language lower trade costs.
o: Rises with both economies' size and falls with distance and trade costs
APE-078.x:
Basis: Tinbergen (1962) – gravity model; Anderson & van Wincoop (2003).
Analysis: Bilateral trade ∝ (GDP_i × GDP_j) / distance – rising with both economies' size and falling with distance and trade costs. FTAs, shared borders, languages and colonial ties lower trade costs → more trade. Used to estimate FTA and tariff effects.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

APE-079.q: Average export prices rise 3% and volumes 8%. By how much does export value rise (%, 2 decimals)?
APE-079.x:
Basis: Applied international economics (price–volume decomposition).
Working: Value = price × volume → growth = 1.03 × 1.08 − 1 = 1.1124 − 1 = 11.24% (approximation 3 + 8 = 11%).
Analysis: Splitting export growth into price (3%) and volume (8%) gauges quality: volume growth reflects real demand, price-driven growth can reverse with commodity cycles (rice, coffee, rubber).

APE-080.q: The terms of trade improve when:
APE-080.e: The same export volume buys more imports.
o: Export prices rise faster than import prices
Import prices rise faster than export prices
APE-080.x:
Basis: International economics (terms of trade = export price index / import price index).
Analysis: Terms of trade improve when export prices rise faster than import prices → the same export volume buys more imports → higher real national income. E.g., oil exporters when oil prices rise.
Distractors: B is volume, not price; C – depreciation usually worsens terms of trade; D is the reverse (deterioration).

APE-081.e: PMI is a diffusion index measuring direction of change versus the prior month.
o: Operating conditions deteriorated versus last month (below 50)
Output is at a record high
APE-081.x:
Basis: S&P Global – Vietnam Manufacturing PMI (diffusion index methodology).
Analysis: The PMI is a composite diffusion index (new orders 30%, output 25%, employment 20%, suppliers' delivery times 15%, stocks of purchases 10%) from purchasing-manager surveys: > 50 improvement on the prior month, < 50 deterioration. A PMI of 48 → mild deterioration versus last month.
Distractors: B and C – the PMI doesn't measure percentage output change; D is wrong.

APE-082.q: A PMI above 50 means the absolute level of production is high.
APE-082.e: False. It shows improvement on last month; after a deep slump, PMI > 50 can coexist with low output.
APE-082.x:
Basis: S&P Global PMI methodology.
Analysis: False. PMI > 50 shows only month-on-month improvement (more firms reporting increases than decreases), not absolute output levels. After a deep slump, several months above 50 may still leave output below pre-crisis levels. Check the industrial production index (IIP) for levels.

APE-083.q: Quarterly GDP grows 1.5% q/q (seasonally adjusted). What is the annualised rate (%, 2 decimals)?
APE-083.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (annualised growth; US BEA convention).
Working: Annualised = (1 + 1.5%)⁴ − 1 = 1.015⁴ − 1 ≈ 1.06136 − 1 ≈ 6.14%.
Analysis: The US reports quarterly GDP at seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR); Vietnam reports year-on-year. Three different figures: 1.5% q/q, 6.14% annualised, and y/y (depending on the last four quarters) – align before comparing.

APE-084.q: This year's y/y growth is very high mainly because last year's level was very low. This is:
APE-084.e: Also look at q/q changes and pre-crisis levels.
o: A low-base effect – be careful extrapolating
APE-084.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (base effects).
Analysis: Very high y/y growth mainly because last year was very weak (e.g., Vietnam's Q3/2021 lockdown → Q3/2022 growth of 13.7%) → a low-base effect, not a durable trend; extrapolate cautiously. Also check seasonally adjusted q/q growth and comparisons with pre-crisis levels (2–3-year CAGR).
Distractors: B concludes hastily; C – it isn't error; D is unrelated.
Note (company analysis): the same applies to EPS growth – off a low base, use multi-year CAGR (as in PEG).

APE-085.q: Q1 GDP grows 5% and Q2 7% y/y; both quarters had equal GDP a year earlier. What is first-half y/y growth (%)?
APE-085.e: With equal weights: (5 + 7)/2 = 6%. In practice weight by each quarter's size.
APE-085.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (weighted cumulative growth).
Working: With equal year-earlier quarter sizes (1 each): this year's first half = 1.05 + 1.07 = 2.12 versus 2 → up 6%; equivalent to (5 + 7)/2 = 6%.
Analysis: In reality quarter sizes differ (Q4 is usually largest) → weight by size: g = Σ(w_i × g_i), where w_i is quarter i's share a year earlier. A simple average is right only with equal weights.

APE-086.q: Comparing February with January data in Vietnam (e.g., industrial output) is easily misleading mainly because of:
APE-086.e: Use seasonally adjusted data or combine the first two months.
o: Seasonality, especially Lunar New Year falling in different months each year
APE-086.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (seasonal adjustment – X-13ARIMA-SEATS; the Tet effect).
Analysis: Lunar New Year falls in January or February depending on the year → working days in Jan–Feb vary widely → comparing February with January (or year-earlier) is distorted. Use Tet-adjusted seasonally adjusted data or combine the first two months for comparisons.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the cause.

APE-087.q: Select ALL checks before using an economic figure for decisions:
APE-087.e: Rule: source – date – definition – unit – period – comparability.
o: Only use headline numbers shared on social media
APE-087.x:
Basis: Applied statistics; IMF Special Data Dissemination Standard.
Analysis: Before using data: (A) definition and coverage (e.g., system-wide credit or only commercial banks); (B) comparison basis – y/y, q/q, YTD; (C) nominal or real; (D) preliminary or revised, and revision risk.
Distractors: (E) Headline figures on social media often lack context and may be wrong.
Note: The principle Source → Date → Definition → Unit → Period → Comparability.

APE-088.q: A firm borrows at 9%; its own output prices rise 6% a year. What is the approximate real borrowing cost measured in its output prices (%)?
APE-088.e: 9 − 6 = 3% (approx.). The relevant real rate for a firm uses its sector's output prices, not just CPI.
APE-088.x:
Basis: Managerial economics (real rates in output-price terms).
Working: Real borrowing cost ≈ 9% − 6% = 3% (exact 1.09/1.06 − 1 ≈ 2.83%).
Analysis: For firms, the relevant real rate uses their own output prices (debt service depends on selling prices), not just CPI. Firms with falling prices (sector deflation – steel, property in downturns) face high real rates even with unchanged nominal rates.

APE-089.q: A manufacturing inventory-to-sales ratio rising for many months usually signals:
o: Weakening demand, risk of production cuts and discounting to clear stock
APE-089.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (inventory/sales ratio – US Census; the Kitchin inventory cycle).
Analysis: A rising inventory/sales ratio for months → goods sell slower than produced, demand weakens → firms will cut output and discount to clear stock → margin pressure and write-downs (CAS-001). Confirm with new orders (PMI): falling orders plus rising inventory is a clear negative.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

APE-090.q: Nowcast: electricity consumption rises 10%; assumed elasticity of power demand to GDP is 1.5. What GDP growth is implied (%, 2 decimals)?
APE-090.e: 10/1.5 ≈ 6.67%. The elasticity varies with economic structure and weather.
APE-090.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (nowcasting with high-frequency data; electricity–GDP elasticity).
Working: Implied GDP growth = power consumption growth / elasticity = 10% / 1.5 ≈ 6.67%.
Analysis: Vietnam's power–GDP elasticity has been about 1.5–2 (falling as the economy shifts to services and saves energy) and varies with weather (heatwaves lift household use) and sector mix → use only for quick estimates, alongside other indicators.

APE-091.q: A strong rise in machinery and equipment imports is often a leading indicator of investment and production expansion in coming quarters.
APE-091.e: True. Rising raw material imports also signal production and export orders.
APE-091.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (capital goods imports as leading indicators).
Analysis: True. Surging machinery and equipment imports → firms are expanding capacity → output and exports rise in coming quarters. Rising input imports (electronic components, fabric, fibre) signal upcoming production–export orders. Falling capital-goods imports are a warning (APE-077).

APE-092.q: CPI jumps in a month mainly due to administered healthcare and tuition price increases. To judge pressure on monetary policy, focus on:
APE-092.e: Administered price shocks are usually one-offs, not demand-pull inflation.
o: Core inflation – the underlying trend excluding administered and volatile items
APE-092.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics; the statistics office's core inflation method (MCR-029).
Analysis: CPI rising from administered price changes (healthcare, tuition) is a one-off administrative shock – not demand-pull or monetary inflation. To gauge monetary policy pressure, focus on core inflation (excluding food, energy and administered prices) – the underlying trend.
Distractors: B is dominated by a one-off; C and D aren't inflation measures.
Note: Watch for second-round effects (expectations, wages) if adjustments are repeated.

APE-093.q: Business planning: nominal GDP is forecast to grow 10%; income elasticity of category demand is 1.2; market share is unchanged. By how much should revenue grow (%)?
APE-093.x:
Basis: Managerial economics (revenue forecasting via income elasticity – MIC-021).
Working: Revenue growth ≈ elasticity × income growth = 1.2 × 10% = 12% (assuming constant relative prices and market share).
Analysis: Sectors with elasticity > 1 outgrow the economy when incomes rise but fall harder in recessions. Forecasts need GDP scenarios (Bear/Base/Bull) and tested share and price assumptions.

APE-094.q: An importer has a large USD payable in 6 months and the FX outlook has many uncertain scenarios. A basic risk management solution:
APE-094.e: Hedging aims to stabilise cash flow, not to profit from FX.
o: Buy USD forwards or options for material obligations, plus flexible pricing clauses with customers
APE-094.x:
Basis: International finance (FX hedging); Circular 02/2021/TT-NHNN (credit institutions' FX transactions – forwards, options).
Analysis: A large USD payable in 6 months with uncertain rates → hedge: buy forward (locking the rate – removing uncertainty at the cost of forward points – APE-095) or buy USD calls (protection if the rate rises, upside kept if it falls, at a premium); add flexible pricing clauses with customers (natural hedge). The aim: stable cash flow, not speculation.
Distractors: B and D speculate; C leaves material risk open.

APE-095.q: A USD 1 million payable is due in 6 months. Spot is 25,300 and the 6-month forward 25,600. What does locking the forward cost versus today's spot (VND million)?
APE-095.e: (25,600 − 25,300) × 1,000,000 = VND 300 million – the 'insurance premium' for removing FX uncertainty.
APE-095.x:
Basis: International finance (forwards – CIP: MCR-081).
Working: Forward cost versus spot = (25,600 − 25,300) × 1,000,000 = 300 × 1,000,000 = VND 300,000,000 = 300 million (≈ 1.19% over 6 months).
Analysis: The 300 forward points reflect the VND–USD rate differential (CIP), not an FX forecast. It's 'insurance' removing uncertainty; if spot in 6 months exceeds 25,600 the hedge wins, otherwise it 'loses' versus not hedging – but the goal is stability, not prediction.
Check: 300 / 25,300 ≈ 1.19% ✓.

APE-096.q: Leading indicators predict the exact timing of recessions in all cases.
APE-096.e: False. They give false signals and variable lags; use them probabilistically and in combination.
APE-096.x:
Basis: Economic indicators (Stock & Watson 2003 – reliability of leading indicators; Samuelson).
Analysis: False. Leading indicators are noisy, give false signals (the 2022–2024 yield-curve inversion – MCR-071), have lags that vary across cycles and get distorted by policy or shocks. Use them probabilistically, combine several (composite LEIs) and update with new evidence (Bayes – BAN-031) rather than drawing certain conclusions from one.

APE-097.q: GDP grows strongly on FDI exports while real retail sales grow slowly and taxes from domestic firms are weak. A reasonable reading:
APE-097.e: Investment decisions should rest on each sector's own drivers, not just headline GDP.
o: Two-speed growth: strong FDI exports, weak domestic demand and local firms – domestically focused businesses should be cautious
APE-097.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (analysing uneven growth).
Analysis: High GDP from FDI exports while real retail grows slowly and taxes from domestic firms are weak → uneven ('K-shaped') growth: a strong FDI export sector, weak domestic demand and local firms. Domestically focused firms (retail, consumer, property) warrant caution; invest on sector-specific drivers, not headline GDP.
Distractors: B and C contradict the facts; D jumps to conclusions.

APE-098.q: Select ALL indicator groups for an investor's monthly macro dashboard:
APE-098.e: A dashboard should link to decisions (asset allocation, leverage), not noise.
o: Credit growth, interbank rates, deposit rates
Exchange rate, FX reserves, trade balance
APE-098.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (macro dashboards).
Analysis: Needed groups: (A) growth – GDP, PMI, industrial production; (B) prices – CPI, core inflation; (C) money and liquidity – credit, interbank and deposit rates; (D) external – FX, reserves, trade balance. The dashboard must tie to specific decisions (asset allocation, leverage, cash weight).
Distractors: (E) Social-media likes are noise.
Note (FERGASITOR Level 7 Automation): an auto-updating dashboard with alert thresholds linked to margin-reduction rules is feasible.

APE-099.q: Under a constant-growth model, fair P/E = 1/(r − g) (ignoring payout). With g = 5%, if the cost of equity r rises from 12% to 13%, what is the new fair P/E?
APE-099.e: Before: 1/0.07 ≈ 14.29; after: 1/0.08 = 12.5 → down about 12.5% from a 1-point rise in the cost of capital.
APE-099.x:
Basis: Valuation (Gordon model – BAN-045; P/E = 1/(r − g) ignoring payout, per the question).
Working: Before: P/E = 1 / (0.12 − 0.05) = 1 / 0.07 ≈ 14.29; after: 1 / (0.13 − 0.05) = 1 / 0.08 = 12.5 → down (14.29 − 12.5) / 14.29 ≈ 12.5%.
Analysis: A 1-point rise in the cost of capital cuts fair P/E by about 12.5% with unchanged earnings – rate-driven valuation compression. Sensitivity grows as (r − g) narrows (growth stocks – long 'duration', APE-047).
Note: The standard formula is P/E = payout × (1 + g) / (r − g); the question simplifies.

APE-100.q: In a top-down approach (macro → industry → company), when data show tightening liquidity, rising rates and slowing credit, the most prudent action is:
o: Cut leverage, favour firms with strong cash flow and safe balance sheets; wait for policy reversal signals
APE-100.x:
Basis: Applied macroeconomics (top-down analysis); risk-management principles.
Analysis: Tight liquidity, rising rates and slowing credit → higher cost of capital, valuation compression (APE-099), margin-call risk (APE-048). Prudent actions: cut leverage; favour firms with strong cash flow and safe balance sheets (low debt, ample cash); wait for policy-reversal signals before raising exposure.
Distractors: B and C add risk just as conditions worsen; D ignores the macro layer.
Note: Survival > Risk control > Capital preservation > Compounding > Maximum return; the rule to cut leverage first when trend indicators deteriorate.
